newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe hopes tax reform will break French gloom.
newsitem.headline: Juppe hopes tax reform will break French gloom.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe hoped to snap France out of a mood of gloom over near-record unemployment and economic stagnation by outlining plans for a five-year income tax cut on Thursday, aides said.

Political sources said the conservative premier had brought forward the announcement due next week partly to distract attention from Wednesday's sombre news that the economy shrank in the second quarter of this year as consumer spending slumped.
He also aimed to unite his restive centre-right coalition ahead of what trade union leaders have threatened to make a "hot autumn" of labour unrest over layoffs and public spending cuts.
Juppe, whose government has raised the tax burden by 120 billion francs ($24 billion) since taking office in May 1995, was to broadcast a prime-time statement at 8 p.m. (1800 GMT).

Francois Leotard, leader of the centre-right Union for French Democracy (UDF), junior partners in the ruling coalition, said after meeting the prime minister that the tax cuts would amount to 75 billion francs ($15 billion) over five years.

Ministers said Juppe would announce a simplification of the complex and inequitable income tax system, riddled with special breaks for everything from owning shares in merchant vessels to investing in France's Caribbean and South Pacific territories.
Special allowances for some 80 professions, including journalists, and tax relief on mortgage interest payments, were expected to be phased out.
Juppe has also promised at least 20 billion francs ($4 billion) in income tax cuts in 1997, some of which may be offset by increases in excise duty on tobacco, alcohol and petrol.
Finance Minister Jean Arthuis and Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure were to give more details of the tax package on Friday.

While voters want to hear their tax burden is finally going to fall, financial markets will be watching to see how the government plans to cut taxes while bringing the 1997 public sector deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product -- from at least four percent in 1996 -- to qualify for a single European currency.

Ministers said Juppe's five-year plan would reduce the number of people who pay any income tax and gradually lower all tax rates, cutting the psychologically important top rate of 56.8 percent to below 50 percent by the end.
The prime minister appeared to have had some initial success in his psychological offensive. French media on Thursday headlined the imminent tax cut rather than the economic downturn.

With the prospect of unemployment continuing to rise while he has to make unpopular budget cuts to bring the deficit down, Juppe has little other hope to offer voters ahead of 1998 parliamentary elections.

Opinion polls show public support for Juppe and President Jacques Chirac rose slightly in August, apparently due to tough government action against illegal immigrants, but a majority of voters continue to disapprove of their performance and expect the economy to get worse this autumn.
By spreading the planned tax cuts over five years, the Right will seek to persuade voters in 1998 that they will only reap the full benefit if they re-elect the conservative coalition, analysts said.

The Socialist opposition has tried to discredit the tax reform in advance by saying Juppe has already taken 120 billion francs ($23.59 billion) from the poor and now plans to give back less, primarily to the rich, while continuing to raise taxes on goods which all French people consume.
